selected_story: Java4Shell: a security startup says AI found a critical Java bug in about an hour, for under $200. Oracle has patched it.
youtube_title: AI found a critical Java bug in 1 hour? Java4Shell explained in Hinglish
why_it_won: Highest trend score of the eligible stories. The one-hour, under-$200 figure is a real surprise for ordinary viewers; Java touches a large share of Indian IT work; and there is one clear action (update Java). It scores lower on credibility than the OpenAI launch because the speed and cost are Calif's own unverified account, so the script attributes them and adds Oracle's 'difficult to exploit' counterpoint.

uncertainties: The one-hour and under-$200 figures are Calif's own and have not been independently checked.
Severity is disputed: Oracle 8.1 and 'difficult to exploit', Calif 9.2. OX Security estimates under 0.12% of JVMs are at risk of code execution.
Which AI was used is disputed (Codex per Calif, GPT-6 Cyber per the New York Times). The script says only 'AI'.
'No confirmed attacks' was true at research time on 18 November. Re-check on the day you post.
Calif's write-up and Oracle's advisory were not opened directly from this environment; open both before recording.
script:
Ek AI ne Java mein ek critical bug sirf ek ghante mein dhoondh liya. Kharcha? Do sau dollar se kam.

Yeh claim hai security startup Calif ka. Bug ka naam Java4Shell. Java par banks, airlines, aur shayad aapki company ka backend chalta hai.

Oracle ka patch aa chuka hai.

Lekin panic nahi. Oracle khud kehta hai exploit karna mushkil hai, aur abhi tak koi real attack confirm nahi.

Asli sabak: bug dhoondhna ab sasta ho gaya hai. Patch late karna mehenga.

Developer ho? Aaj hi Java update karo.
recording_instructions: iPhone rear camera, 4K 30 fps, vertical, eye level, wireless mic on. HDR video off if possible (the pipeline tone-maps HDR, but that path is untested on real iPhone HDR footage).
Leave the top third of the frame clear above your head: title cards sit there. Captions sit just below centre.
Say the first line fast and flat, then pause on 'Kharcha?'. Slow down at 'Lekin panic nahi'.
If you fluff a line, pause one second and repeat the whole sentence. The editor keeps the last complete take of each sentence.
Record one full run. Do not stop the recording between retakes.
Save the file as footage/incoming/2026-11-18.mov, then run: creatoros edit footage/incoming/2026-11-18.mov --date 2026-11-18
visual_references: 0-4s: face to camera with the title card '1 GHANTA. $200.' and a 'CLAIM: CALIF' label (generated by the pipeline).
Calm beat: 'Oracle: difficult to exploit' and 'No confirmed attacks, as of 18 Nov' (generated).
Takeaway split: 'Bug dhoondhna: sasta' against 'Patch late: mehenga' (generated).

Optional real source material you capture yourself: a screenshot of Calif's post and of Oracle's advisory page. Add them to the edit plan as image overlays and list them in assets/licensed/manifest.json.

linkedin_caption:
A security startup says an AI model found a critical Java flaw in about an hour, for under $200 in compute.

The bug, Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), sits in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. Oracle patched it on 17 November.

Some perspective: Oracle rates it 'difficult to exploit', one independent estimate puts under 0.12% of JVMs at real risk of code execution, and no attacks are confirmed. The speed and cost figures are Calif's own and unverified.

The bigger shift is economic. If finding serious bugs now costs hours and a few hundred dollars, slow patch cycles become the expensive part.

If you run Java 17 or later on x86 servers, check your version this week.
x_caption: Calif says AI found a critical Java bug in ~1 hour for under $200. Oracle has patched Java4Shell; no attacks confirmed, and Oracle calls it hard to exploit. Bug-finding just got cheap. Slow patching just got expensive.

factcheck.story: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Calif says AI found a critical Java flaw in about an hour

claims.text: An AI model found the bug in about one hour, at a token cost under $200
claims.note: Calif's own account. Not independently checked. Calif's write-up was not opened directly from this environment.

claims.text: The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and sits in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder
claims.note: Consistent across independent security vendors. Oracle advisory not opened directly.

claims.text: Oracle released a fix in its 17 November 2026 Critical Patch Update
claims.note: Fixed versions reported: Java SE 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1. Re-check against Oracle's advisory before publishing.

claims.text: Oracle rates the flaw 8.1 (CVSS 3.1) and describes it as difficult to exploit
claims.note: Calif rates it 9.2 (CVSS 4.0). Severity is disputed between the two.

claims.text: No exploitation in the wild has been confirmed
claims.note: True as of research time on 18 November 2026. Must be re-checked on the day of publishing.

claims.text: Java runs at banks, airlines and many company backends
claims.note: Widely documented general fact; the '90% of Fortune 500' figure is deliberately not used.

claims.text: Which model was used: Codex (Calif) or GPT-6 Cyber (New York Times)
The NSA network outage is linked to Java4Shell
claims.note: No reporting links them. Not used.

access_limits: X, Instagram, YouTube and most news sites cannot be opened from this cloud environment; research used web search results only.
Likes, reposts and views could not be observed for any post and are marked UNKNOWN.
Post times are decoded from the X status IDs, not read from the posts.
The script duration is an estimate at an assumed 150 words per minute; no text-to-speech voice here reads Roman Hinglish reliably.
